outline.heading: Focus on Properties of the Value and Policy Functions A portion of the course is dedicated to exploring the properties of the value and policy functions. I provide a systematic way to prove properties of the value function such as concavity, monotonic- ity, supermodularity and differentiability, and derive monotonicity conditions regarding the policy function. Some of these results are based on the foundational works of Topkis (1978, 1998), while others are more recent developments from Light (2021). 3. Introduction to Reinforcement Learning The course also includes an introduction to reinforcement learning, focusing on theoretical aspects. I provide the proof of the convergence of Q-learning type algorithms to the optimal Q-function. This technical analysis follows the classic treatment of Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis (1996) but offers a simplified and more focused perspective. I also introduce Q-learning with function approximation, and with online search. Additionally, I present policy gradient methods using the average reward case, which is somewhat more natural and easier to analyze than the discounted case. I discuss policy gradient theorem and the performance difference lemma for the average reward case and simulation methods with policy gradient using the average reward case. Furthermore, I provide the proof of convergence of the policy gradient method to the optimal policy in the tabular case. This result appears to be new in the average reward case, albeit similar (and simpler) than the well-studied discounted case. * The lectures may have mistakes and typos. Please contact me if you found any. * Exercises are given in the end of each lecture. Partial solutions are given in the end of the document. 3

outline.heading: Metric Spaces We first recall the definition of a metric space and the basic concepts of open sets and Cauchy sequences. Definition 1.1 A metric d on a nonempty set X is a function d
outline.body: X × X → R satisfying three properties: 1. Positivity: d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x, y ∈ X, and d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y. 2. Symmetry: d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y ∈ X. 3. Triangle inequality: d(x, y) ≤ d(x, z) + d(z, y) for all x, y, z ∈ X. The pair (X, d) is called a metric space. For x ∈ X, the open ball around x with radius r is given by B(x, r) = {y ∈ X : d(x, y) < r}. A subset A of X is called open if for every x ∈ A there exists r > 0 such that B(x, r) ⊆ A. A is closed if the complement of A given by X \ A is open. A sequence {xn } of a metric space (X, d) is said to converge to x ∈ X (typically denoted by xn → x or lim xn = x) if lim d(xn , x) = 0. A function f : (X, dx ) → (Y, dy ) between two metric spaces is called continuous if f −1 (O) := {x ∈ X : f (x) ∈ O} is an open subset of X whenever O is an open subset of Y .1 A family of sets {Ai }i∈I such that Ai ⊆ X is said to be a cover of X if X ⊆ ∪i∈I Ai . If Ai are open for each i, then the cover is called an open cover. If a subfamily of {Ai }i∈I also covers X then it is called a subcover. A set A ⊆ X is compact if every open cover of A can be reduced to a finite subcover. Recall that A is compact in a metric space if and only if every sequence in A has a subsequence which converges to a point of A. In addition, if A ⊆ Rn then A is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. For every set A in a metric space, we let cl(A) to be the smallest closed set that includes A. A metric space (X, d) is called separable if there exists a countable subset S such that cl(S) = X (e.g., R with d(x, y) = |x − y| is a separable metric space as we can let S to be set of rational numbers). 1 You are probably more aware of the equivalent definitions: f is continuous if lim xn = x holds in X implies that lim f (xn ) = f (x) holds in Y or f is continuous if for every point a ∈ X and every ϵ > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that dy (f (x), f (a)) < ϵ whenever dx (x, a) < δ. 10

outline.heading: Probability Spaces A probability space is defined by (Ω, F, P) where Ω is the sample space or the space of all possible outcomes, F is a sigma-algebra and P is a probability measure. The sigma-algebra F contains the sets (sometimes called events) that can be measured. For- mally, F ⊆ 2Ω where 2Ω is the power set of Ω is called a sigma-algebra if the following three properties hold
outline.body: (1) B ∈ F implies Ω \ B ∈ F, i.e., it is closed under complements. (2) Ω ∈ F. (3) If B1 , B2 . . . is a countable collection of sets in F then ∪i Bi ∈ F, i.e., it is closed under countable unions. The probability measure P is a function that assigns to any set in F a number between 0 and 1, and satisfies (1) P(Ω) = 1, P(∅) = 0. (2) If B1 , B2 . . . is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint P sets in F, i.e., Bi ∩ Bj = ∅ for all i, j, then P(∪i Bi ) = i P(Bi ). For the rest of these lectures, Ω will be endowed with a metric d and (Ω, d) will be a separable metric space. Let B be a collection of subsets of Ω. The smallest sigma-algebra containing all the sets of B is called the sigma-algebra that is generated by B. For any collection of sets B the sigma-algebra that is generated by B exists (see exercises) and is denoted by σ(B). We are now ready to define the Borel sigma-algebra. Definition 1.2 Let (Ω, d) be a metric space. The Borel sigma-algebra on Ω is the sigma-algebra that is generated by all the open sets of Ω. A set is called a Borel measurable set if it belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra. A function f : Ω → R is called a Borel measurable function if f −1 (V ) := {ω ∈ Ω : f (ω) ∈ V } is a Borel measurable set in Ω for every open set V in R. Remark 1.1 When Ω is countable then we will assume it is endowed with the discrete distance, i.e., d(x, y) = 1 if x ̸= y and d(x, x) = 0. In this case every set is open (why?), and hence, the Borel sigma-algebra is 2Ω and every function is Borel measurable. Remark 1.2 The Borel sigma-algebra is the smallest sigma-algebra such that every open set is measurable, so it is the smallest sigma-algebra such that every continuous function is measurable. 12

It is not hard to see that if p is continuous then k(s, a) = S f (s′ )p(s, a, ds′ ) R is u.s.c and bounded whenever f is. Hence, if p is continuous it is also u.s.c. outline.heading: Filtration A filtration is a sequence of sigma-algebras that represent the accumulation of information over time. Formally, a filtration {Fn }n≥0 is a collection of sigma-algebras such that
outline.body: F0 ⊆ F1 ⊆ F2 ⊆ · · · ⊆ F. Each Fn represents the information available up to time n. A filtration can be defined by random variables as the sigma-algebra generated from them. For a sequence of random variables {Xn }n≥0 , the natural filtration {Fn } is given by: Fn = σ(X0 , X1 , . . . , Xn ), which is the smallest sigma-algebra with respect to which X0 , X1 , . . . , Xn are measurable. We say that the sequence {Xn }n≥0 is measurable with respect to a filtration {Fn } if Xn is Fn -measurable for each n. For example, Suppose that Xn are Bernoulli coin flips, where Xn = 1 if the coin flip results in heads (with some probability p), and Xn = 0 if it results in tails and define Fn = σ(X0 , X1 , . . . , Xn ). Then F0 is generated by X0 and contains all possible information outcomes of the first coin flip. It consists of the sets {∅, Ω, {X0 = 0}, {X0 = 1}}, where Ω is the sample space of all possible outcomes. Fn includes information from all Xk for k ≤ n. For example, a random variable Yn = X0 + X1 + . . . + Xn (the total number of heads up to time n) is measurable with respect to Fn , as it is a function of the outcomes X0 , . . . , Xn but is not measurable with respect to Fn−1 . 4.2.3 Martingales, Sub-Martingales, and Super-Martingales Martingales are a powerful tool in probability theory due to their convergence properties and wide range of applications. They provide a framework for modeling many different probabilistic settings and are instrumental in the analysis of stochastic processes. Martingales are extensively used in financial mathematics for modeling asset prices and in the development of pricing algorithms for derivatives. outline.body: Match driver type 2 with request type 1. • a22 : Match driver type 2 with request type 2. • a0 : No match (the system waits for the next time step). • a3 : Match both drivers with both requests simultaneously. Note that this action is only avail- able in the state (1,1,1,1). When a matching action is taken, the matched driver and request are removed from the system, transitioning the state vector components corresponding to the matched driver and request from 1 to 0. However, after each time step, there is a probability pid that a removed driver di will reappear in the system (transitioning from 0 to 1) and a probability pir that a removed request ri will reappear (transitioning from 0 to 1). If the no match action (a0 ) is chosen, the state remains the same, or a driver di may reappear with probability pid if it was absent, and a request ri may reappear with probability pir if it was absent. When a3 is taken, the system transitions directly to state (0, 0, 0, 0), removing all drivers and requests from the system. After this action, each driver and request has a probability pid and pir of reappearing, transitioning the respective components of the state vector from 0 to 1. The reward from action a0 is zero, from a3 is x3 and from aij is xij for i = 1, 2, j = 1, 2. The discount factor is β ∈ (0, 1). Assume that β = 0.99.
